title: The Immaculate Heart of Mary
hookLine: the Saturday after the Sacred Heart, Mary's heart is honored
tomorrow: The first martyrs of Rome (30 June)

cards: Shepherds crowd in around a manger at night, out of breath, talking over each other. Angels, they say. A sky full of them.
Everyone who hears it is amazed. And in the middle of the noise, the young mother says nothing. Luke turns his camera to her face for one sentence, then moves on.

On a Friday in the weeks after Pentecost, the Church honors the Sacred Heart of Jesus. The next day, a Saturday, it turns to that quiet face, and the heart behind it. Today, the Immaculate Heart of Mary.

teach.h: SHE KEPT THESE WORDS IN HER HEART.
teach.b: Here's the sentence. In the Douay-Rheims: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Kept, like something put away safely.
Pondering, turning it over, the way you turn a stone in your hand. Luke says it again when Jesus is twelve, after he's found in the Temple: his mother kept all these words in her heart.
Luke never gives us a speech from Mary at those moments. He gives us her heart, working. A third line is harder.
When the baby is presented in the Temple, an old man named Simeon blesses them and says to Mary: "And thy own soul a sword shall pierce."

That's why pictures of the Immaculate Heart often show a heart with a sword through it, or ringed with roses, or burning with flame. Love, and the cost of love, in one picture. The name trips people up.
Catholic teaching holds that Mary was kept free from sin from the first moment of her life; that's the Immaculate Conception, a separate feast in December.
This day is about her heart: the inner life of a woman who said yes, kept watch, and stood at the cross.
Over time the devotion grew, and some Catholics connect it with the reported apparitions of Mary at Fatima, in Portugal. Not every Christian keeps it.
Orthodox Christians honor Mary in their own ways, and some Protestants read these same verses as a picture of faith without a feast for her heart.
For Catholics, the two hearts side by side, the Son's on Friday and the mother's on Saturday, say something plain: her heart was pointed toward his.

how: The Church keeps the memorial of the Immaculate Heart of Mary on the Saturday after the Solemnity of the Sacred Heart; some Catholics pray the rosary on the day, and some keep a devotion of first Saturdays.

games.q: you're Mary. shepherds burst in with news of angels, and everyone is amazed. what does Luke say you do?
o: tell everyone what the angel told you.
keep these words and ponder them in your heart.
ask the shepherds to leave the baby to sleep.
games.why: Luke gives no speech from Mary here: she keeps all these words, pondering them in her heart.

practice: Bring to mind a mother you know, your own, someone who mothered you, or a friend raising children now, and think of what she might be carrying that she doesn't say out loud. Hold it with her, quietly.
If you pray, entrust her to Mary, whose own heart held so much in silence; if you don't, simply wish her rest and company.

wordCard.voice: Immaculate Heart, the Catholic devotion to Mary's inner life, honored on the Saturday after the Sacred Heart.

carryVoice: Your line: her heart. Some of the biggest things are kept, not said. Until tomorrow.
